title: Should NOT Have Sold The Family Business | Down The Plughole Podcast ep1

segments.text: They were just waiting for me to fail.
I took it on board and I killed it within a couple of years.
If I knew then what I know now, we'd never have sold.
When my father died, everybody shut the doors on us.
Money's [music] important to everybody, but ain't my god.
More is not always a profitable thing.
I should never have done it.
The same man did knock me for money. We had no more work. We're finished.
Talk for me.
Talk to me. Talk to me.
>> [laughter] >> Why did you get these budget chairs?
>> They're all right. They're good. They're good. Good.
Why am I so low down? I can't sit in this. Why am I No, I've got to get a different chair, man. I can't sit in this.
>> get a different chair, bro?
>> I think there's a chair over there.
What was that now, mate?
Look at this Look at this Look at this.
And you know what?
I'll just sit on it, Michael. It's fine.
I've got a thing over here. I'm here.
I'm in it Oh, no, I'm not. I can't get no further.
>> I have it as well.
>> You've got to sit in the car, haven't you?
There we go.
That any better?
>> [clears throat] >> You're You're a bit of a large chap, aren't you?
What's happened?
>> [laughter] >> I'm Daniel.
This is Ashville.
And this is Mr. Michael O'Donovan. For those of you who watch Ashville videos, you would have seen this man in many of
videos over the years hurling insults at me and helping me out whenever he can.
Now, jokes aside, >> No more insults.
Michael is both like a friend, older brother, and a bit of a father figure to me.
He to the best of my understanding, he learned a lot from his father, which he passed down to his sons. And when I
started in this industry, it was very difficult for me to get advice from anyone.
And my townie actually introduced me. For those of you who don't know, uh my townie is the engineer/
technician who does all of the Ashville work when we're rebuilding, when we're repairing, when we're doing maintenance.
He is from Limerick in Ireland, and Michael is from West Cork. My townie introduced me to Michael, and since that point, I was really surprised cuz I'd never met the man before, and he
actually gave me a D-ring for my skip chains. Whenever I called him and asked him for advice, he picked up the phone.
And then one fateful day, there were two Scania salesmen trying to both sell us lorries, so we went on a trip to Sweden, and I happened to be on a jolly up with Michael.
And from that point, we were kind of I won't say inseparable because we're both very busy fellows finding our own ways in the world, but Michael has always been very helpful to me and has
worked hard to keep both of my feet on the ground. So, everything I've been through, Michael's probably been through it and done two or three cycles of it
already. So, it's always good to get his insight.
>> Mhm.
>> And Michael, I want to start off with you telling me how and when O'Donovan started.
>> Right.
1957, my mother and father left Ireland, come to London.
Went to Cricklewood.
rented a house, I believe. There's actually a book about this house and all the people they rented it with.
There's actually a book out there somewhere on me dad. [snorts] And then me dad started with a crowd called Mangans. They used to do garages.
And he picked up from there and he just he was working with them for quite a while. And then in about 1959, I think it was, he bought his first bulldozers, which was a 951. And went
doing demolition. Cracked on from there.
Got to find out a bit more about what was going on, how to work how the how this job worked. Then he decided he'd buy his first lorry, which, if you look to my right, is a Thames Trader.
And that is what he started with, one of them. So he had a one machine, Thames Trader. Then he bought another Thames Trader.
Then he bought a Chinese six Dodge.
And then he bought another Thames Trader. So then he had four lorries and a machine and cracked on with the demolition.
Then from there it just grew.
Then we got into the skips in 1972, which were for I remember recall the day that he brought the skip lorry down the street on a Sunday afternoon.
I thought, "What is this thing? What what's he doing with this? What Who's got skips? Who does skips?" Obviously the Thames Traders were well and truly gone by then.
You had the Would you have had the Maggy Dodge? Yes, you would have had the Maggy Dodge, which he bought a few second hand ones.
Then he bought some brand new.
The Scammell outside was the main vehicle my dad run. We had a big yard in King's Cross.
We cracked on with one skip lorry and then we From one skip lorry it went to two, it went to three, it went to four.
And then all of a sudden, I think at one stage he had 20-odd skip lorries on the road.
Plus there was 28, 29 tippers.
There was 360s, which not a lot of people had 360s. We had a lot of caterpillars.
Mom looked after the house. Dad looked after the work. Took me to work at the age of 12.
That's where I learned my trade. If you didn't do it right, you got told.
You don't not doing it right. Do it this way. Don't do it that way. Which I took on board.
And then we cracked on from there.
And then obviously it just snowballed from there. Got a ground working firm.
Started another company, a separate to his own company here.
He had a a ground working company, demolition company, and obviously tippers, skips, and a plant hire company.
One was called Summerstown Plant, which would run the plant.
There was Highfield Demolition, which was the demolition side. Then you had D.J. O'Donovan and Sons, which was the tipper side and the skip side. And then obviously we were probably one of the
first people to have a transfer station in King's Cross.
We were transferring the rubbish from the skips to tippers.
And then obviously like everything else, it snowballed again.
And it got bigger. We moved to a new yard.
Then we bought our first yard. And then everything just went from there. Went And then in 1985,
we got a shock. My dad passed away.
And then I was given the keys to crack on.
>> How old were you?
>> I was 22 at the time.
Plus I got to say, and I would say it to everybody, only for me dad, we wouldn't be where we are today. So we had a good stepping stone.
I listened to everything he said.
Maybe an odd time I didn't listen, but most of it I did listen to.
And we cracked on from there. I see how we could go forward. I watched what he done. I seen how he done it. Then my younger sister come on board.
Obviously, she run the office. I run the yard.
Uh my other sister run the skips. And my brother run the yard as well with me.
Or a different yard, I should say. We had a yard in Scrubs Lane at the time.
And then obviously our Donovans waste disposals come from this.
>> So, you said that at 12 years old your dad had you working. You're meant to be at school at 12 years old. So, how did that work?
>> Uh what happened was Uh if you got up in the morning early and you were standing by the bed, you could go to work.
>> So, that What do you mean?
>> If you were up before my dad, >> Yeah.
>> which my dad had a nickname called Sputnik, so you had to be up early to beat him.
So, if I was at start of the bed, he'd take me to work. But if he refused to take me to work, there used to be a driver of his used to wait for me at the bottom of White Hart Lane. And I'd run down
the road.

I'd throw my briefcase or my bag into the front of the lorry, take my tie off, take my coat off, put my hand in my bag, put my jumper on, and I would spend the day with him in the lorry. He would drop me back at
White Hart Lane. I would then get a bus to Alexandra Palace, get on the train, and go to the yard.
My dad used to say to me, "Have a good day at school." I said, "Great day at school, Dad."
>> So, where did your mom think you were?
>> School.
>> Your mom thought you were at school?
>> Yeah.
>> So, at 12 years old you was actually out on the job with your dad's drivers learning the trade.
>> Learning the trade and listening and watching, seeing how things were done.
So, yes, I did miss miss the education side of things.
But um has it done me any harm?
Yes, a little bit, but not really.
>> How did missing school and parts of education, how has that affected your reading and writing?
>> Very much so.
But now, do I need I could still do a bit of it.
The writing side of it, I'm not the best, but I can still write.
>> But you know what? I'll say something for you. You can count.
>> Yes, I can count.
Very easy.
I watched my dad count. He used to very good at counting.
>> Tell me about your relationship with your dad.
>> Oh, we were like that. We never like I was with him all the time.
We were with him I was near enough with him 24/7, you might as well say.
>> Tell me what a day would be like on a Saturday, because obviously dad thinks you went to school Monday to Friday.
What would that look like? And where would you be before Spotnik woke up?
>> Um early days, in the very early days, if he had a demolition job, he would bring me to my job would be to burn the timber. Or go to go through go

into the building, pull the bond through the building, no gloves, no nothing, grab hold of an old rusty old bond, take it up through the building, bring it out the other side, throw it down to him. He'd pull the building over,
and that was what our day. And then I'd spend the rest of the day throwing wood in the fire.
That would be my day's work.
And I would get rewarded maybe a breakfast.
And a bottle of Coke and a bag of crisps on the way home.
>> And what machines could you drive and what age did you learn to drive lorries?
>> I was driving lorries at the age of 13.
I actually drove a brand new lorry for my dad when I was 15.
I could drive any machine, not very good, but I could drive it. I could get it out of my way and I could use it if I needed to. If I needed to load myself or load lorries, I could do it.
>> And how would you say watching your dad and the companies grow, and your dad getting up in the in the and going to
work every day. How would you say it af- it affected you? What did it instill in you?
>> That the only way you're going to get anywhere in life if you get out of bed and go to work.
And obviously graft.
Obviously my dad saved, graft, saved, graft. So, the moral to the story is get up, go to work, you'll have money.
If you don't want to go to work, you won't have money.
>> And how did it affect the family when he passed suddenly? Was it Did Did you know it was coming or it happened sudden?
>> It just happened overnight. We just got a phone call. I'll never forget it, the 12th of September on a Thursday. I got a Me Shaymus uh fit was with us 40-year 42 years he was with us.
>> Your townee?
>> Yeah, Shaymus. Yeah, my townee, yeah. He was with us 42 years. And he and myself went to the testing station, took two lorries back, and I never used to go to pub during the week. And he said, "Do
you fancy a beer?" I said, "Go on then."
So, we run over to the pub, and I think I just got the first drink, and I got a phone call to go to the hospital at the Archway, and that's when we found out about me dad.
And it was just a shock cuz no one My dad was as fit as a fiddle.
Just couldn't understand it.
But, hey-ho, what What's about today saves people, what wasn't about then. Maybe if he had tablets to do this, tablets to do that, we don't know.
>> And at 22 years old, you've basically become head of the family.
>> Yeah.
>> You're the oldest?
>> Oldest of the family. It took me a couple of weeks to get over what had happened, but once I got my head round it and I thought, "Well, it's I can't let this fail."
So, I thought I got to get stuck in. So, I wouldn't let let it be said that I took it on board and I
killed it within a couple of years. I thought this has got to go This has got to work.
So, I went and graft myself on a tipper.
My sister was in the office. We just grafted.
Uh me and Sheamus, God rest his soul. He um as we call him my towny as well he was.
He would stay till God knows at night time to make sure the lorries were ready next morning.
We tried to keep the fleet out as long as we could.
We scrimped and scraped, got past everything, worked 24/7. We were doing 7 days a week cuz I thought this cannot fail. I missed a lot of time with with my boys.
But it was a case of either that or we wouldn't have what we have today.
>> And over the years in part two shall we call it, while you were growing the firm after your dad had passed and you were head of the family,
how did things change in regard to health and safety compliance? How did that change the job? Cuz many a time when we've spoken about it, when I was
running tippers you'd say, "Lad, you missed Lad, you missed the golden age when when there was money in lorries.
Now it's just a race to the bottom." How did things change over the years in running like a haulage waste business?
>> When we were doing it, there wasn't this legislation. And I remember one time that you were getting and I'm talking a lot of years ago back in the
late '80s.
Late '80s, early '80s.
You were getting 300 something pound a load to go to Camden Town and that was >> Of muck?
>> Of muck. And I don't >> You can't get that now in a tipper.
>> Thank you.
We were getting that and we were and we were moaning about going to Camden Town for a load of muck.
And we were tipping in the likes of Broxbourne, which we thought was far away.
Now look where you're going with a load of muck. And look what you're getting for the load of muck.
Didn't last long, but it lasted long enough that you could earn a few quid.
And then you didn't have all this fours, you didn't have all this this hoops you got to jump through now to have a tipper. Long as you had an operator's license and tax, off you
went.
Tips that time were 10 and 15 quid. I remember tipping stone was 6 pound a load.
>> Wait, so you were taking a load of muck away for 300 quid and tipping it for what?
>> If you were If you were taking it to Broxbourne, I think at Broxbourne that time was I think about 18 pound a load.
>> Those margins and you could do four a day easy.
>> Oh my goodness. And this was when?
>> Back in the late '80s. Early '80s late '80s, I can't remember the exact time.
We had another time then we were doing the Cambridge roundabout they were doing the Cambridge roundabout and there was a shoot out on the A10, Spencer Kings.
I think that was something like 10 or 15 pound a load. And that was open from 6 in the morning till 6 at night.
>> Would you say in those years that those those are the years when O'Donovan pushed on >> Yeah, we made money. Because you could
make money.
>> And would you say that you reinvested most of it in the business?
>> 90% of it went back into the business.
As soon as we made a couple of quid we bought a newer lorry or we got something newer than this. The new Iveco come out and this one was We still had a couple of these old ones and we had a new
couple of not brand new cuz you wouldn't buy brand new lorries at the time.
We run a lot of Ivecos at the time cuz they were good lorries.
But you earned money. You had money the end of the week. You You had money to show for your week's work. And the skips were good at the time.
I don't think the skips were about that time, probably 90 to 100 quid for a skip.
But, every time you tipped one, there was some There was There was There was something to salvage out of that skip.
>> What was the general mentality of people who worked for you in the yard, of lorry drivers, machine drivers, laborers? How does it differ from today?
>> Well, used to today now is completely different. When we had drivers I've got to say, though, a lot of my dad's drivers, when they when I took over, did leave because they didn't want to
work with myself.
Cuz obviously I was 100 mile an hour.
New fellows come in, younger fellows come in and took over. They wanted to go grafting.
We used to be leaving the yard at 6:00 in 6:00 at the morning.
Heading to Spencer King's to tip a load of muck, and you were still on the road at 1/2 5:00 in the evening coming back to the yard, trying to get a load on for the morning.
So, the driver mentality then was they didn't care. They were out all night They were out all day.
There wasn't the rules weren't as stringent as what they are now. Like, we could work every Saturday.
We could work Sunday.
>> And did drivers and machine drivers did they have more or less of an understanding of how a vehicle or a machine actually work?
>> I would say then more of an understanding. Half of them, if they did get a If there was a breakdown, they could ring and tell you what the problem was. It's X, it's Y, it's Z.

So, you could I could tell Seamus this is wrong with the lorries. This has come off. This has gone. This has come loose. This is lost. And he would go and he would grab something off another lorry if there was one in the yard, or
he'd go and get a part, and he go and fix it.
He never come home without bringing a lorry home. Whether he brought it back on a straight bar or he fixed it, it never was left on the road overnight. And drivers then weren't
weren't clock watching.
They didn't really care. The ones The ones I had around me didn't care. In the later years, even recently, a lot of the drivers there were with us quite a while, 20-odd years, 10 years, 15 years.
Most of them were there quite a while.
So, we had a good I've got to say all the way through, I've always had a good team of drivers around me.
>> And would you say the drivers and machine drivers that went the extra mile for you, would you say that they worked for O'Donovan or they thought they worked for you personally?
>> I would say they probably thought they worked for me personally, cuz we had an understanding.
Cuz of course some of them, obviously, you know you've got You have You've had it yourself. You've got the ones that won't that'll hide around the corner.

But I know all the tricks, cuz I used to drive a lorry. So, I'd know what corner they'd be hiding around. So, I'd appear around that corner. And I'd stand outside the yard, and I'd just look at my little watch, and I'd be tapping my watch.
Cuz I know they could go and do another one.
Or go and put one on for the morning, or wash their lorry, or do something.
But if they were finished and we had no more work, you're finished.
But don't hide.
If the work's finished, the work's finished. If the work's not finished, let's do the last one.
The last one's the one that earned you the money.
>> When I started documenting work that Ashville were doing, and I started with the whole social media
journey, I was probably one of the first, if not the first, to actually document on a weekly basis what it was like to try and run
a haulage, a plant firm, and in the beginning, I got a lot of resistance, and people were saying a lot
about me. I I ignored it.
But, when everybody had something to say, you weren't bothered, and you sort of embraced it when everyone else kind of said, "What's he doing? He don't know
what he's doing anyway. He's been at it 5 minutes. Why doesn't he shut his mouth? He's telling everybody all the secrets."
>> There is no secrets.
>> You You didn't You half encouraged me.
As somebody who's been in the business, it's not like you were in the business 5 minutes. You've been in it since you were 12 years old. So, why were you
happy to be on camera? Why were you happy to encourage me? And why did you embrace kind of the new digital wage
earlier than everybody else did?
>> See, what the problem is, our job has got a big problem.
Because I've been in it a long time, and I've seen it from start to finish.
Everybody's worried about what everybody else is doing. Instead of keeping their own camp going, they're all worried about what Daniel's doing.
I used to get phone calls. I told you I got phone calls of people.
"Why are you doing this? Why are you doing that?" Well, why am I doing it?
What's it got to do with you what I'm doing?
You sell your boat, I sell my boat.
If my boat takes on water, and I sink, it's my own doing.
It's not anybody else's doing. But, they do This job seems to breed people that worry about what other people are doing.
And then, instead of them watching their own boat, their own boat takes on water.
And then, their own boat sinks, and they think, "Oh, sugar.
I shouldn't have been worried about him, or worried about that one, or worried about that one."
And that is what their problem is.
This This job just I don't know. I just can't understand it. Everybody just worries and jealous. Someone sees someone with a new lorry or you've done something like your videos.
We have a crack.
That's all about What's this is what this job's about. Can't be coming to work every morning going big long face on you. Even though some mornings you want to come to work and pull your hair out.
You got to embrace the job, get on with it.
And hope you come out at the end of the day with a bit of profit. And don't worry about what John down the road is doing or Bill's doing up the road.
If they've had a bad day, that's not your problem.
But what would you be telling secrets?
You put a load of muck on the back of a tipper, you take it to the tip and tip it.
That's all you were telling them.
You take it You put a ballast in the back of a volumetric, you put a bit of water in it, put a bit of cement in it, and it comes out the end, and it goes in the trench.
What were you telling them?
If they didn't know that, they shouldn't be in the job.
So, the way I look at it is mind your own.
Don't worry about what Daniel's doing.
Don't worry about what Michael's doing.
Sell your own boat.
And make sure it doesn't take on any water.
>> But why Why are you Why are you happy to be to to be on camera and to see young fellas doing >> It's a bit of crack.
It's a bit of fun.
Getting it out there, telling people what we do, how we do it, what we do every day, how we take the piss out of each other.
Oh, I'll take it out of you, though.
Mhm.
It ain't my fault you went down the plug. I was >> [laughter] >> All right, WE WE WE WERE SERIOUS for so long. It was It was It was bound to happen, wasn't it? It was bound to happen.
>> And he was boasting about how his jaw was bigger than mine. Now, his jaw's only a lot size of a shoe box, but yeah.
Who knows about Who knows anything about that?
What can we do? What can we do? But yeah, we're friends, and we crack on, and we do things together. If there's a problem, we'll ring, we'll have a chat.
>> Would you say there's there was any pivotal point in O'Donovan's journey when you were
like when you when you said to yourself we're we're moving on here. Like like we're we're stepping it up a level. Like we're doing well.
We're going in the right direction. Was there any particular moment when you realized that?
>> When we when my sister took the bull by the horns and decided we're going to do all this push it out there and get this done and get the do it this way. Where we had to
get all the accreditations and do all this which I was like, "Do we really need this?" But yes, we do need that. We needed 4's
gold. We needed I ISO whatever it is.

Then we needed ISO 72 million. You wanted all these and you had to have all the accreditations. Just the They had to have the CPCA terms and conditions and you had to have this and have that. She pushed it on from there. That got us
into more sites and all of a sudden we're doing work for proper money.
Where other people couldn't go in there cuz they never had the accreditations.

So then I thought, "Here we go." So then we started buying lorries at five and six at a time. I bought 10 new Scania skip lorries and I bought 10 new ones in it. Which they weren't the cheapest skip lorry in the world.
But we bought 10 at a one time. Then I cracked on again.
We bought the yard in Alberton. Put a new system in there, new trommel system.
Probably not what's out today cuz obviously everything's come more advanced again. But it got us going.
The yard got us going. The yard was one of the busiest I think and we only used to have our own lorries tipping in there. And we were doing 240 250 skips a day.
And we were turning out. And we were we were recycling this, recycling that.
Then obviously we were showing near enough 90-odd percent recycling.
We were baling. We were baling and that was that was going for incineration to power plants.
>> Was there ever a time when you thought this isn't going well and we're in trouble here or has it always been on the up, smooth sailing?
>> No, there was one Christmas. I can't remember when it was.
I've done a job for a so-called friend of mine.
I won't mention the site.
Um there was a lot of muck away coming out of there. We had I think we had 20-odd of our own on there plus other other other lorries doing work elsewhere. With 20-odd of our own,
we had I think uh another seven, eight pirates probably running out of there. It wasn't it was only a short run to the tips. I wasn't but we had two 20-tonners loading.
And it was a very, very, very, very busy job.
And at one stage we were over we were owed over 100,000 pound. We'd done a demolition job as well, which we were owed money on.
We'd done another couple of jobs and everybody owed us money and all of a sudden it's coming near Christmas time and we're struggling to pay bills cuz no one's paying us.
So I was walking about looking at windows thinking how are we going to get over this?
So I went to the so-called friend of mine and I managed to get some money off of him by going there and begging for my own money that I earned.
And he did and the same man did knock me for money.
I rang the crowd up we'd done the demolition job for. They said that we didn't do this. So I said what do you think this is? So I took a reduction on the job. We got paid for that.
I'd done the same with the other couple of jobs. I gave them all money back. We didn't earn any real profit that year or that that for doing them jobs, but
we actually got paid.
So, we got over that Christmas and I thought No, this cannot happen again.
This cannot happen again.
Cuz that could have brought us under. It would have been all hands to the pump. The boat would have been taken on water.
There would have been a few other people that wouldn't have been able to be paid.
We could we wouldn't have been able to pay them.
So, it would have been a nasty turnaround for everybody. We would have owed them. We were owed. They would have been owed. Everybody would have been owed.
>> So, so you're saying that you could have gone down the plug hole.
>> We could have gone down the plug hole right behind you.
Then hence I'd be driving around in a number 73 bus.
And the train to Hemel Hempstead.
You've got Oyster card nowadays, all right.
He's had it right off.
>> If this Michael could call 22-year-old Michael and get him on the phone for half an hour,
what would you say to him?
>> I couldn't say a lot to him.
Cuz you couldn't have done a lot.
Once I got over the initial shock of me dad dying, I just sat myself down and I said to myself, right, this cannot
fail.
So, there's nothing I could have told I could nothing I could have told him now that I didn't already know then.
Cuz I thought this is this cuz people would as you have just said, people were watching me.
They were just waiting for me to fail.
But I thought I can't I got to do it for me dad and the family that we cannot fail.
So, I put me shoe through the headlight and kept going.
>> So, there's no advice that you would give him.
>> advice whatsoever cuz I just stuck my head into the drive mode and I just thought we got to keep going.
And I've got to say 10 out of 10 to the few people that were around us at the time that stuck with us.
They all helped.
They all got stuck in.
A lot of people now a lot of them have passed away. A few of them have a lot good few of them have passed away. The few that left neither here nor there.
But the few that stuck with us helped us a lot through.
>> And would you have done anything differently?
>> Not a thing.
Cuz I am where I am today due to it.
Otherwise, I wouldn't be where I am today.
I'd probably be driving a lorry for someone.
Very badly.
Cuz I don't want to put them out of business as well.
You've been driving for you.
>> [laughter] >> A few years back, O'Donovan, the main O'Donovan business, uh was sold.
And you now work in a different capacity just with your sons and advising as your sons are doing their own thing with
Enfield Skips and O'Donovan Brothers.
What sort of change was it for you the day when the transaction went through and you didn't have to be in Tottenham at that yard in the morning?
>> It took me a long time to get over that bit cuz I still went to the yard.
And I don't and I still cannot answer that question why I used to go to the yard, but my sister was working for this the company that took us over.

And she was running the office side of things, so I thought I'll keep an eye on the yard for a which is I why I done. I don't know why I done it, but but I had Kaylee Plant was in the same yard at the time, so I had me machines down there and
I was still doing looking after my own bits, plus looking after what she had to look after. But then when they let my sister go, which um I thought was a big mistake on their behalf, but what do
I know?
Uh I decided I'd leave as well. So, we all left left them to it.
>> But how did it feel when >> I should never have done it.
>> Wow.
>> I'm at a loss I'm at a loose end now.
